title: Would you trust an AI scientist?
question: How much scientific decision-making should an autonomous AI researcher be allowed to control?
explicit: Research questions should remain accountable to human scientific judgment.
Independent replication should precede reliance on autonomous discoveries.
Permit autonomous hypothesis generation within a bounded research programme.
inferred: Bounded delegation would preserve meaningful human scientific control.
scenario: an AI proposes an unexpected biological mechanism and asks to redirect the laboratory
test: compare independently reproduced results, missed alternatives and the effort required to challenge a proposal

title: Could robots run the laboratory?
question: Should laboratories allow robots to plan and execute experiments with minimal human supervision?
explicit: Laboratory automation should have explicit intervention and shutdown responsibilities.
An experiment can be technically successful while answering the wrong research question.
Start with task-limited autonomous laboratories and independent review.
Allow broader autonomy only after the laboratory can explain failed experiments.
Preserve hands-on training even when robots can execute the work.
inferred: Task boundaries would keep laboratory failures containable.
Removing hands-on practice would weaken future researchers’ experimental judgment.
scenario: a robotic laboratory keeps optimizing a measurable output while ignoring an anomalous result
test: test error recovery, operator intervention and whether trainees can diagnose a failure
additional_claims: An accountable operator should be able to interrupt a running experiment.
Automation evaluations should include experiments that produce unexpected results.
Laboratories should retain a record of discarded hypotheses.
Procurement should preserve access to experimental logs when a vendor leaves.
Safety review should be independent of the team rewarded for laboratory throughput.

title: Longevity: longer life or healthier life?
question: Should public research funding prioritise healthier ageing or attempts to extend maximum lifespan?
explicit: Public longevity research should report functional outcomes alongside survival.
Access and affordability should shape priorities for publicly funded interventions.
Prioritise additional healthy years over record-breaking lifespan extension.
Keep a smaller programme for high-risk research on maximum lifespan.
Allocate a protected share of funding to social conditions that affect ageing.
inferred: Funding healthy years would favour interventions that preserve everyday functioning.
scenario: a proposed intervention promises longer survival but leaves its effects on independence unresolved
test: compare functioning, burden on carers, accessibility and the distribution of benefits
additional_claims: Research priorities should include outcomes reported by older people themselves.
Public trials should assess the burden of repeated treatment.
A lifespan target should not be treated as a substitute for a quality-of-life target.

title: Fusion dreams or a better grid?
question: How should an energy research budget balance fusion ambitions against improvements to existing grids?
explicit: Energy funding should distinguish research potential from deployable reliability.
A portfolio should make the cost of delayed delivery visible.
Protect long-term fusion research while expanding near-term grid work.
Concentrate marginal funding on grids until fusion milestones are independently met.
Reserve funding for energy access rather than only national technology leadership.
scenario: a budget committee must choose between another experimental facility and neglected transmission upgrades
test: compare delivery milestones, reliability improvements and communities reached by each allocation
additional_claims: Funding milestones should distinguish a scientific demonstration from an affordable power system.
Grid projects should be evaluated for the communities whose reliability improves.

title: Who gets to touch the thermostat of Earth?
question: Who should be allowed to authorise research or deployment of solar climate intervention?
explicit: Climate-intervention decisions should include countries exposed to possible cross-border effects.
Research governance should distinguish observation from deployment.
Allow independently overseen research without treating it as permission to deploy.
Require a separate international decision before any sustained deployment.
Give disproportionately exposed communities a meaningful power to refuse participation.
inferred: A research boundary could remain enforceable despite pressure to deploy.
Ordinary representation alone might fail to protect disproportionately exposed communities.
scenario: an emergency creates pressure to turn a limited research programme into an operational intervention
test: test governance boundaries, accountability for unexpected outcomes and whose objections can change the decision
additional_claims: No state should gain unilateral authority to deploy a global climate intervention.
Outdoor experiments should publish their stop conditions before they begin.
Affected countries should have a route to challenge proposed experiments.
Research governance should include who would be responsible for terminating a deployment.

title: Carbon removal: public service or offset machine?
question: Should publicly supported carbon removal be used to compensate for continued emissions?
explicit: Carbon-removal claims should keep storage durability and measurement uncertainty visible.
A removal purchase should not erase the obligation to reduce avoidable emissions.
Prioritise removal for residual emissions with independently verified storage.
Keep reduction targets separate from any purchased removal credits.
Exclude public subsidies for removals that mainly prolong an avoidable high-emissions activity.
inferred: Separate accounting would prevent removal purchases from weakening reduction obligations.
scenario: a firm requests a subsidy for removals while postponing an available emissions reduction
test: compare additionality, durability, uncertainty and what the buyer would do without the credit
additional_claims: Public purchasing should separate verified removal from promises of future removal.
Communities hosting removal facilities should be able to contest local burdens.

title: Could a city retreat from the coast?
question: When should a coastal city invest in protection, adaptation or voluntary relocation?
explicit: Coastal planning should disclose who bears the costs of each option.
Residents should receive credible alternatives before a relocation decision.
Combine protection with funded voluntary relocation in the most exposed areas.
Prioritise protection where relocation would destroy irreplaceable community ties.
Guarantee renters a relocation offer rather than compensating property owners alone.
inferred: A credible relocation offer would permit a genuinely voluntary choice.
Owner-only compensation would leave some residents unable to move safely.
scenario: a neighbourhood must decide whether to rebuild after repeated disruption or accept a relocation offer
test: compare security, affordability, community continuity and the choices available to renters
additional_claims: Relocation offers should cover tenants as well as property owners.
Compensation should account for the loss of community ties.
Public authorities should state which services they would maintain during a retreat.

title: Bring back the wild: who decides?
question: How should a region decide whether to reintroduce a large predator?
explicit: Reintroduction plans should define responsibility for losses and conflict resolution.
Local participation should affect the plan rather than merely approve it.
Begin a monitored reintroduction with explicit compensation and review rules.
Delay release until affected communities can challenge the proposed safeguards.
Protect the option of coexistence without requiring every resident to welcome reintroduction.
scenario: a reintroduction proposal promises regional benefits while concentrating immediate concerns in a few farms
test: compare conflict resolution, compensation delays, monitoring and the distribution of local benefits
additional_claims: Rewilding agreements should specify who bears losses if wildlife damages livelihoods.

title: Meat without animals: a public bet?
question: Should governments subsidise cultivated meat, plant-based food or neither?
explicit: Food innovation should be assessed on the system it would replace.
Public support should disclose production uncertainty and distributional effects.
Fund competing low-impact protein approaches against common evaluation criteria.
Prioritise established alternatives while cultivated-meat production remains uncertain.
Protect small producers from being locked out of a subsidised food transition.
inferred: Common evaluation criteria would permit a fair comparison between protein approaches.
A subsidy programme could otherwise concentrate the transition in a few firms.
scenario: a public fund must choose between a demonstration facility and scaling familiar lower-impact meals
test: compare credible production pathways, affordability, access and effects on existing producers
additional_claims: Public funding should make pilot results available beyond the funded company.
Food-safety review should be separate from judgments about consumer appeal.
Scaling plans should disclose energy and water requirements.
Animal-free production should not be assumed to settle environmental questions.
Public investment should preserve routes for small food producers.
Ingredient labelling should identify the production method without implying unproven benefits.
Production trials should report the cost of maintaining clean facilities.
Worker transition plans should accompany support for new production systems.
Procurement trials should include foods that people would choose to eat repeatedly.
Public contracts should limit dependence on a single proprietary production process.
Funding should include a comparison with plant-based alternatives.

title: If AI could translate animals, should we listen?
question: What should change if AI appears able to interpret meaningful animal communication?
explicit: A claimed animal translation should be tested against alternative explanations.
An interpretation should not be treated as animal consent.
Use independently tested interpretations to improve animal-welfare decisions.
Keep welfare protections even when a model appears to report a positive response.
Prohibit entertainment uses that deliberately provoke distress to obtain interpretable signals.
inferred: Validated interpretations would track animal welfare rather than only human expectations.
scenario: a model produces convincing human-language descriptions of animal sounds but the evaluation is disputed
test: compare predictions against independently designed behaviour tests and document ambiguous cases
additional_claims: Translation systems should distinguish observed animal signals from human interpretations.
Public demonstrations should disclose when a translation has not been independently tested.

title: Digital afterlives: comfort or exploitation?
question: Should people be able to create an AI replica of a deceased person?
explicit: A digital replica should remain visibly distinct from the person it represents.
Consent should cover posthumous use rather than assume permission from available messages.
Permit limited replicas when prior consent and revocable access are documented.
Prohibit replicas when the represented person did not provide meaningful consent.
Prevent replicas from soliciting money or manipulating an emotionally dependent user.
inferred: Visible disclosure would prevent users from mistaking a replica for the represented person.
scenario: a family wants a comforting replica while relatives disagree about consent and commercial access
test: compare consent records, boundaries of use, withdrawal options and responses to emotional dependence
additional_claims: A person should be able to prohibit a conversational replica during their lifetime.
A replica should disclose that its replies are generated rather than remembered.
Surviving relatives should not automatically inherit the right to alter a replica.
Providers should offer an exit that does not require continued subscription payments.

title: Brain data: the last private space?
question: What rules should govern devices that infer information from brain activity?
explicit: Brain-data use should be limited to purposes that a person can meaningfully understand.
Refusing a brain-sensing device should not itself count as evidence against a person.
Permit voluntary narrowly specified uses with strict secondary-use controls.
Exclude brain-based inference from employment selection and routine policing.
Give people a practical right to delete derived profiles as well as raw recordings.
inferred: Purpose limits would remain enforceable when new inferences become possible.
Keeping derived profiles would undermine meaningful deletion of brain data.
scenario: a voluntary device collected for one purpose later supports a new inference requested by an employer
test: compare enforceable purpose controls, refusal consequences and deletion of derived information
additional_claims: Brain-data permission should be specific to the proposed use.
Employers should not make neural monitoring a condition of ordinary work.
A person should be able to withdraw permission without losing unrelated services.
Derived inferences should be covered by the same protections as raw recordings.
Access records should show which organisation used a neural recording.
Public standards should distinguish medical use from workplace surveillance.
Data collected for rehabilitation should not be reused for advertising.

title: Editing future generations
question: What would justify permitting heritable genome editing?
explicit: Heritable-editing decisions should separate demonstrated capability from moral permission.
A decision should account for people who cannot participate in the original consent.
Require a separate publicly accountable authorisation process before any permitted use.
Keep a prohibition while essential uncertainties and governance questions remain unresolved.
Do not make access to support contingent on whether a family accepted an editing option.
inferred: Public authorisation would represent the interests of affected future people.
An editing option could otherwise reduce support for people living with the targeted trait.
Long-term follow-up would make harms to later generations observable before broad use.
scenario: a technically persuasive proposal reaches a regulator while families disagree about the social meaning of the intervention
test: compare consent limits, alternatives, public accountability and protection for existing communities
additional_claims: A future child cannot provide consent before a heritable intervention.
Permission for a clinical trial should not automatically permit commercial rollout.
Alternatives should be assessed for the specific condition under discussion.
Public debate should distinguish preventing a severe condition from selecting a preferred trait.
Long-term monitoring should include who would pay for follow-up care.
Trial oversight should include people living with the condition being discussed.
Eligibility rules should not imply that existing disabled lives are less valuable.
Access rules should be settled before a successful intervention is offered commercially.
An intervention should not be called reversible when its inherited effects cannot be recalled.
Parents should receive information about uncertainty without pressure to participate.
Independent review should consider effects on subsequent generations.
A clinic should not be able to set the public eligibility standard by itself.

title: An AI tutor for every child?
question: How should schools use highly capable AI tutors without losing the human parts of education?
explicit: Educational evaluation should include relationships and agency as well as test performance.
A student should be able to challenge an AI tutor’s interpretation of their needs.
Use AI tutors as teacher-supervised support rather than a default replacement.
Allow broader tutor autonomy only after independent evaluation in the relevant setting.
Preserve a non-AI route for students who do not benefit from the system.
scenario: a tutoring system improves a chosen metric while teachers worry that students stop asking independent questions
test: compare learning transfer, agency, relationships and the experience of students who opt out

title: Four days of work: who wins?
question: When should an organisation adopt a four-day working week?
explicit: A working-time trial should measure workload intensity as well as output.
Benefits should not depend only on whether a role is easy to reschedule.
Run a protected trial without using unpaid extra hours to preserve output.
Offer role-specific shorter-hour options where a common four-day schedule does not fit.
Include contract and shift workers in any sharing of the gains.
inferred: A protected trial would prevent nominal time reductions from hiding unpaid work.
scenario: office teams want a shorter week while service coverage depends on shifts and contractors
test: compare total hours, intensity, coverage, retention and who receives the time benefit
additional_claims: Pilots should report whether workload is reduced or merely compressed.
Assessment should include workers whose shifts cannot be shortened easily.
Pay protection should be explicit rather than assumed in a four-day offer.

title: Your genome as a forecast
question: Should consumer genetic-risk forecasts be used outside clinical care?
explicit: A genetic forecast should display uncertainty and the population limits of its interpretation.
A person should control whether a consumer result reaches another institution.
Restrict institutional use until the specific decision has independent validation.
Keep consumer exploration available without permitting automatic institutional decisions.
Prohibit insurers and employers from requiring consumer genetic-risk disclosure.
inferred: Decision-specific validation would identify when a genetic forecast is useful for that decision.
Nominally voluntary disclosure could become effectively compulsory in unequal relationships.
scenario: a consumer receives a persuasive risk score and an institution requests access before making an unrelated decision
test: compare population transfer, uncertainty communication and the real freedom to refuse disclosure
additional_claims: A genetic forecast should describe which population informed its interpretation.
A person should be able to decline a forecast while retaining ordinary care.
Counselling should distinguish increased risk from a predicted diagnosis.
Results should not be shared with employers without a separate decision.
Screening programmes should state how an uncertain result changes clinical action.
An updated interpretation should not silently replace the original report.

title: A city on Mars: whose rules?
question: How should a permanent Mars settlement govern itself while preserving scientific and ethical responsibilities?
explicit: Settlement rules should distinguish scientific stewardship from a claim to exclusive ownership.
Residents should have a meaningful way to contest life-support decisions.
Give residents democratic control within independently reviewed stewardship obligations.
Retain shared oversight for decisions with irreversible consequences beyond the settlement.
Preserve protected areas even when expansion would be more convenient without them.
scenario: residents want to expand while scientists dispute whether the proposed area should remain undisturbed
test: compare infrastructure accountability, contested decisions and preservation of future research options
additional_claims: Commercial operators should not have sole authority over essential life-support access.

title: Robotaxis: convenience for whom?
question: What should a city require before allowing large-scale autonomous taxi services?
explicit: Transport evaluation should consider street use and accessibility rather than trips alone.
Public authorities should retain enforceable oversight of service changes.
Permit staged deployment tied to independently evaluated public-interest outcomes.
Limit expansion until underserved areas and disabled riders have credible service access.
Protect public-transport funding rather than assuming private fleets will replace it.
inferred: Deployment conditions would remain enforceable when the fleet operator becomes indispensable.
scenario: a fleet offers convenient journeys in profitable areas while requesting broad access to public road space
test: compare accessibility, street use, underserved areas and dependency on one operator
additional_claims: Operators should publish how passengers can obtain help during a stalled journey.
Access evaluation should include passengers who cannot use a smartphone.

title: Could citizens govern with an AI adviser?
question: Should citizens’ assemblies use AI to organise evidence and propose policy options?
explicit: Assembly members should be able to inspect which arguments the system excluded.
An AI-generated option should remain a proposal rather than a decision.
Use AI for evidence organisation while reserving deliberation and judgment to citizens.
Require an independently prepared account alongside the AI’s presentation.
Preserve minority reports rather than reducing assembly output to a single recommendation.
inferred: Inspectability would let citizens detect consequential omissions in the evidence account.
A single recommendation could otherwise erase unresolved minority reasoning.
scenario: an assembly receives a beautifully concise AI briefing that participants suspect has omitted a difficult alternative
test: compare traceability, omissions, time for challenge and the survival of minority reports
additional_claims: Citizens should be able to inspect the sources behind an AI briefing.
Briefing systems should display credible alternatives rather than one recommended answer.
A facilitator should be able to correct a misleading briefing during deliberation.
The public record should separate citizen recommendations from AI-written suggestions.
Participants should be able to deliberate without using the adviser.
System evaluation should include groups with different levels of digital literacy.
AI suppliers should disclose conflicts of interest relevant to a policy question.
A citizens assembly should retain authority over its final recommendation.

title: Open science at the edge of danger
question: How should institutions decide when to restrict a powerful biological research tool?
explicit: Restrictions should identify the capability of concern rather than rely on a field’s reputation.
A governance decision should consider both scientific access and misuse uncertainty.
Use independently reviewed access tiers with proportionate monitoring and appeals.
Keep selected capabilities restricted when credible safeguards cannot be demonstrated.
Protect legitimate researchers in low-resource settings from blanket exclusion.
inferred: Access tiers would reduce the identified risk without simply moving it elsewhere.
scenario: a useful tool raises contested governance concerns and an access restriction would exclude a small research group
test: compare proportionality, meaningful appeals and whether the restriction addresses the identified capability
additional_claims: Restrictions should distinguish a research result from instructions that enable harmful application.
A review should state the concrete harm that withholding information is meant to prevent.
Researchers should have a route to appeal a restriction.
Restricted results should be reviewed again when circumstances change.
Access decisions should not depend solely on institutional prestige.
A public explanation should identify what can still be shared safely.
